findings.claim: Starter skills would not benefit from Docling structure even if it worked, because their citation and navigation model runs on clause numbers the LLM reads from the canonical text stream, and the shipped verification path (normalized_content substring) is the only structure the skills' citations depend on.
findings.evidence: Inference from skills/nda-review/SKILL.md:136 and msa-review-saas/SKILL.md:92,170 (LLM-read structure) combined with PRD.md:425 (verification against normalized_content) and ADR 0006:57-58 (chunker drives off PyMuPDF stream)

q1.bottom_line: "M2 consumption" was a placeholder, not a specified consumer: the only named design that would have read documents.structured_content — PRD §3.3's CitableChunk schema (bbox overlays, structural_role filtering, hierarchy) — shipped in M2 without any of it, built instead on normalized_content substring verification, and the M2 implementation plan never mentions Docling at all; ADR 0006's own language is "may use it," with the stated benefit being merely avoiding a future re-parse. M3-C Tabular Review, the most plausible-sounding "tables" consumer, provably consumes lexical FTS over PyMuPDF-derived document_chunks and never touches structured_content; its "table" is an output grid, not parsed table structure. None of the starter skills reference parser structure — they prompt the LLM to read clause numbers from text. The orphan DE draft's author believed in future M2 readers and a "uniformly v1 corpus," both premises now known false; DE-271 already documents an Apache Tika fallback path, meaning canon itself treats Docling as replaceable.

findings.claim: Q1 (what PyMuPDF gives): the canonical text is plain `page.get_text()` per page joined by a single newline — no headings, tables, lists, or column metadata survive as structure. Heading TEXT survives inline as plain numbered lines.

findings.claim: Q1 (would any shipped capability notice?): chunk boundaries key ONLY on regex sentence terminators `[.!?]\s` and paragraph breaks `\n\s*\n` — never on headings, tables, lists, or columns. Loss of heading levels and list structure is invisible to the chunker by construction.

Test comments contain no known-issue notes. Per instruction: this absence is WEAK evidence of sufficiency — the corpus exercised is synthetic single-column and the user base small.

findings.claim: Q3 (the 10 sample contracts are structurally trivial for PyMuPDF): all rendered from Markdown via Chrome headless with single-column body CSS; each contains exactly one table (the signature block) and no multi-column layout anywhere. Executed PyMuPDF extraction on 2 of the 10 confirms clean single-column reading order with numbered plain-text headings. The NDA README itself flags that the corpus uses 'clean section structure' and doesn't test extraction edge cases.

The synthetic corpus uses clean section structure').

findings.claim: Q1/Q2 (design intent confirms sufficiency-by-architecture): ADR 0006 deliberately drives the chunker off the PyMuPDF stream because Docling offsets are not character-precise, states chunk boundaries are 'an indexing optimisation... not a verification artifact', and stashes Docling output only for M2 'forward compatibility'. The citation invariant is self-consistent under scrambling: verification checks the quote against the SAME flat stream the model was shown, so table interleaving cannot break citation verification — it can only degrade what an LLM reads inside a chunk.
findings.evidence: docs/adr/0006-document-pipeline-architecture.md §Decision 1 (lines 44-89, esp. 'drive the chunker off the PyMuPDF character stream', 'stashed in documents.structured_content... for M2 to consume') and §Neutral (line 254-257 'M1 doesn't read it back'); chunker.py:33-36 ('chunk boundaries are an indexing optimisation... not a verification artifact'); verification.py:170-215. The 'can only degrade LLM comprehension, never citation verification' consequence is inferred from the observed mechanism.

findings.claim: Q1 (where loss WOULD eventually be noticed): real-world contract PDFs with genuine multi-column layouts, pricing/SLA tables, or rate cards would produce interleaved chunk content, degrading what the model quotes in playbook extraction, tabular review, and chat-over-KB — but there is no committed test, corpus document, or issue demonstrating this today, and the shipped Easy Playbook wizard's own acceptance corpus avoids it by design.
findings.evidence: Inferred from: extractor.py:207 feeding flat normalized_content to the LLM; observed signature-block interleaving as the mechanism; sample-ndas/README.md 'does NOT test' caveats; absence of any table-bearing test fixture (api/tests/fixtures/pdfs/_make_fixtures.py builds simple/multipage/two-column prose only).

q2.bottom_line: The PyMuPDF-only pipeline is demonstrably sufficient for every capability shipped today: the entire consumer chain — chunker (sentence-regex boundaries, chunker.py:64-66), embeddings (embed.py), hybrid retrieval (retrieval.py:1-17), citation verification (verification.py:170-215), and playbook extraction (extractor.py:207) — operates exclusively on the flat canonical character stream, nothing reads documents.structured_content (only writers plus the ORM column exist), and the citation invariant is immune to layout scrambling because it verifies against the same stream the model saw. What is demonstrably lost is table cell structure (observed: the corpus's only tables, 2-column signature blocks, extract row-interleaved — benign) and a latent, untested multi-column reading-order risk (the two-column fixture asserts only offset fidelity, never column order). There is zero recorded evidence of chunk-quality or citation-precision problems in docs, .github, tests, or GitHub issues — but this is weak evidence of sufficiency, since the 10 sample contracts are Chrome-rendered single-column Markdown that the NDA README itself admits uses "clean section structure" and does not test extraction edge cases; real-world table-heavy or multi-column contracts have simply never been exercised on record.

No other api dependency touches torch.

findings.claim: CRITICAL GOTCHA (verified by dry-run): tool.uv.sources index pinning does NOT apply to transitive dependencies. A scratch project with only `docling>=1.16,<2` plus the pytorch-cpu index/sources config still resolved torch from pypi.org/simple with all nvidia-* packages (0 occurrences of download.pytorch.org in the lock). Declaring torch and torchvision as direct project dependencies makes the pin bite (13 occurrences, torch resolved as 2.13.0+cpu from the CPU index). So api/pyproject.toml must add torch+torchvision as direct deps (or equivalent) for this to work.

findings.claim: Residual cost after CPU pinning: ~0.45 GB wheels either way; ~78-98 non-app packages still in the SBOM for a feature nothing reads (docling tree is 90-110 packages standalone); the ~696 MB HuggingFace model download at first use is untouched by any of this (models are fetched at runtime, not install time); and install/pull time shrinks roughly proportionally to the 2.45 GB wheel reduction. The GIVEN facts that nothing reads documents.structured_content and 6/6 docs show docling=fallback are unchanged by this option — CPU pinning makes Docling cheap, not useful.

findings.claim: Gotcha — no blast radius on other api deps: with explicit=true the pytorch-cpu index is consulted only for packages explicitly pinned to it via tool.uv.sources, so the rest of the dependency tree keeps resolving from PyPI; the scratch locks confirm only torch and torchvision came from download.pytorch.org. The sys_platform=='linux' marker keeps macOS dev machines (houfu's aarch64 darwin) on normal PyPI wheels, which are CPU-only on macOS anyway.

findings.claim: Gotcha — re-locking floats torch upward on the linux fork: the current api/uv.lock's torch 2.2.2 is most plausibly held down by the darwin-x86_64 resolution fork (torch >2.2.2 ships no macOS x86_64 wheels, and the lock's resolution-markers include x86_64 darwin), and once the linux fork is split off to the CPU index it independently resolved to 2.13.0+cpu in the dry-run. If the maintainers want reproducible behavior they should add an explicit torch version constraint when introducing the pin.
findings.evidence: api/uv.lock:1-14 (resolution-markers include "platform_machine == 'x86_64' and sys_platform == 'darwin'"); api/uv.lock torch block wheels list has torch-2.2.2 macosx_10_9_x86_64 wheel; scratch case-a lock forked to 2.2.2 (darwin) / 2.13.0+cpu (linux). The 'macOS cap is why 2.2.2 was chosen' causal link is inferred, not stated anywhere.

findings.claim: Gotcha — docling 2.x default engine swap and system libs: the docling 2.120.1 default resolution replaced easyocr with rapidocr and pulled opencv-python (full build, 71.1 MB) rather than opencv-python-headless — the full build typically needs libGL/libglib system packages that python:3.12-slim does not ship, so the Dockerfile would need apt additions or a headless override. Docling 1.x kept opencv-python-headless (50 MB).
findings.evidence: Scratch case-b size report: "opencv-python 5.0.0.93 ... 71.1 MB", "rapidocr 3.9.2 ... 27.3 MB", no easyocr in the 110-package lock; case-a report shows opencv-python-headless 4.11.0.86. The libGL-on-slim consequence is inferred from standard opencv-python packaging, not tested in this run.

findings.claim: Gotcha — CPU inference speed is a real but bounded concern: upstream reports put OCR+table-structure conversion at ~18 minutes per 100 pages on CPU (issue #2120), with 3-4 GB RAM spikes and 100% CPU during conversion (issue #2877, discussion #245); layout-only conversion (no OCR) is much faster (~seconds/page). Since lq-ai's Docling pass is a background second pass whose output nothing reads, slow-but-completing is tolerable, but worker timeout and memory limits on the arq/ingest workers should be checked before enabling it for real.
findings.evidence: WebSearch results: github.com/docling-project/docling issues #2120 ("1080 seconds ... for just 100 pages" with OCR+tables), #2877 and discussion #245 (3-4 GB RAM spikes, CPU 100%), discussion #2259. The worker-timeout implication for lq-ai is inferred.

findings.claim: The change surface for Option A is small and lock-only in effect: edit api/pyproject.toml (add [[tool.uv.index]] + [tool.uv.sources] + torch/torchvision direct deps), regenerate api/uv.lock, no Dockerfile change needed — `uv sync --frozen --no-install-project` (api/Dockerfile:25) consumes the index pins recorded in the lock as-is. The uv.lock format in the repo (version = 1, revision = 3) matches what uv 0.12.0 writes, so the toolchain is already current.
findings.evidence: api/Dockerfile:24-25; api/uv.lock:1-2 ("version = 1", "revision = 3"); scratch locks written by uv 0.12.0 use the same format and embed the CPU-index sources; local uv --version = 0.12.0 matches the Dockerfile's pinned copy (api/Dockerfile:9).

q4a.bottom_line: Yes — Docling's cost can be almost entirely removed without removing Docling, and it was measured, not estimated: pinning torch/torchvision to the pytorch-cpu index (supported by the repo's exact uv 0.12.0 toolchain) shrinks the Docling-exclusive wheel payload from 2.91 GB to ~0.45 GB (a ~2.45 GB, ~84% cut, dropping all 12 nvidia-* SBOM entries) while keeping the current docling 1.x pin byte-for-byte unchanged. The one non-obvious trap is that uv's tool.uv.sources pinning ignores transitive deps — the dry-run proved the CPU index is silently ignored unless torch and torchvision are also declared as direct dependencies of the api project. The same CPU pin is equally necessary and equally effective under a docling 2.x upgrade (2.120.1 defaults to the slim/standard install, ~444 MB with CPU torch, OCR/VLM now extras), so CPU-pinning is orthogonal to — and cheaper than — the upgrade decision. Residuals that no pinning fixes: ~0.45 GB wheels and ~80-100 SBOM packages for a feature nothing reads, the ~696 MB runtime HF model download, and CPU conversion at up to ~18 min/100 pages with OCR — Docling becomes cheap, not useful.

findings.claim: Option 1 — pymupdf4llm: gives markdown with heading hierarchy, table detection (Markdown/HTML), and multi-column reading-order reconstruction; the wheel is 176.4 KB; latest release 1.28.2 (2026-08-06, active cadence, backed by Artifex — the same vendor as PyMuPDF we already carry); dual-licensed AGPL-3.0 / Artifex commercial, identical to our existing PyMuPDF posture so zero new license exposure; no GPU; no OCR of its own (scanned docs stay with the Mistral-OCR/PaddleOCR path PRD line 234 already defines). Caveat: recent versions pull in pymupdf-layout (~43 MB binary wheel, GNN layout model, also AGPL/commercial dual) as a dependency for improved results — that is the entire marginal SBOM cost (~2 packages, ~45 MB vs Docling's 80 packages / 2.91 GB). Without the layout package, heading detection falls back to the font-size heuristic (inferred from pre-layout pymupdf4llm behavior).
findings.evidence: PyPI pymupdf4llm page: v1.28.2 2026-08-06, 'GNU AGPL v3 or Artifex Commercial', wheel 176.4 KB, 'Markdown with heading hierarchy... tables to Markdown or HTML... reconstructs natural reading order across single and multi-column pages'; PyPI pymupdf-layout page: 'GNU AFFERO GPL 3.0 or Artifex Commercial License', ~42.9 MB wheels, 'used by PyMuPDF4LLM'. Repo baseline: PyMuPDF already carried per api/app/pipeline/parsers.py (given) and PRD.md:234 ('PyMuPDF for character-precise byte offsets ... AGPL is not contagious through HTTP API boundaries').

findings.claim: Option 2 — unstructured (OSS library): Apache-2.0, v0.25.2 (2026-08-03, active, backed by Unstructured.io). But its PDF structure story splits by strategy: 'fast' uses pdfminer only — no layout analysis, no heading/table detection; only 'hi_res' does real layout via detectron2_onnx model inference (onnxruntime + unstructured-inference + model weights), and hi_res is the only strategy that extracts PDF tables. So to get structure you buy a model-inference stack again (system deps poppler-utils, tesseract-ocr, libmagic plus a large Python extra tree) — a smaller Docling, not an escape from the pattern. Estimated [pdf]+hi_res footprint several hundred MB plus model downloads (inferred; not published as a single number). OCR available via tesseract (ocr_only/hi_res). No GPU required (ONNX CPU) but CPU inference cost per page is real.
findings.evidence: PyPI unstructured page: v0.25.2 2026-08-03, Apache-2.0, [pdf] extra needs poppler-utils/tesseract-ocr/libmagic; docs.unstructured.io partitioning page: '"fast" ... uses pdfminer ... does not perform layout analysis'; '"hi_res" employs detectron2_onnx ... the only strategy that currently extracts tables for PDFs'; 'ocr_only ... Tesseract ... no layout analysis'.

findings.claim: Option 3 — marker (Datalab): output quality is excellent (markdown + JSON block tree with headings, tables, equations) but it is eliminated on license and stack: code is Apache-2.0 while the model weights are a modified AI Pubs OpenRAIL-M — 'free for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue', commercial license required beyond that. LQ.AI is a self-hosted product whose operators include enterprises over that cap, so we cannot ship marker weights as a default parser without imposing a per-operator licensing question — directly contrary to the project's open-source self-hosted posture. Stack is PyTorch + Surya VLM with an inference server (vLLM on NVIDIA GPU, llama.cpp for CPU); footprint is Docling-class or larger (inferred). GPU strongly preferred; OCR built in via Surya.
findings.evidence: github.com/datalab-to/marker README: 'Code: Apache 2.0 ... Model Weights: Modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M ... free for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue'; dependencies 'PyTorch, Surya ... vLLM (NVIDIA GPU) or llama.cpp (CPU)'.

findings.claim: Option 4 — pdfplumber + camelot: both MIT, both tables-only for our purposes. pdfplumber (v0.11.10, 2026-06-15) extracts text with layout options, tables via lines/text/explicit strategies, and precise object coordinates — but no heading semantics, no reading-order model, and explicitly no OCR ('works best on machine-generated, rather than scanned, PDFs'). camelot-py (v2.0.0, 2026-06-04, MIT) is tables-only by design, default backend pdfium with no system deps; scanned-table support requires [ml,ocr] extras (Table Transformer + OCR), which reintroduces model inference. Neither answers the actual gap — headings/clause hierarchy for contracts — so they are complements at best, not a Docling replacement.
findings.evidence: PyPI pdfplumber: MIT, v0.11.10, 'OCR is not supported', tables via '"lines", "text", or "explicit"' strategies; PyPI camelot-py: MIT, v2.0.0, tables-only, 'pip install "camelot-py[ml,ocr]"' for image-only PDFs.

findings.claim: Option 5 — Apache Tika (the PRD's own documented Docling fallback, PRD.md:2784): Apache-2.0, very healthy (ASF-governed, v3.3.2 released 2026-07-16), tika-server-standard jar ~78.1 MB plus a JRE (~200-300 MB container layer, inferred) — dramatically cheaper than Docling but a JVM sidecar in a Python stack. Capability ceiling: Tika's PDF path is PDFBox text extraction emitting XHTML with paragraph-level markup only — no layout model, so no genuine heading hierarchy, table structure, or reading-order reconstruction for born-digital PDFs (inferred from Tika/PDFBox architecture; the project site does not claim layout analysis). It gives robust text + metadata across many formats, i.e. roughly what PyMuPDF already gives us, not the structure Docling was supposed to add. As a *structure* option it is therefore weak; as a many-format text fallback it remains sensible, which is what DE-271's wording ('Apache Tika + custom parser layer') already implies.
findings.evidence: docs/PRD.md:2784 ('if Docling is abandoned, fall back to Apache Tika + custom parser layer'); tika.apache.org: v3.3.2 '16 July 2026', ASF project; mvnrepository tika-server-standard 3.3.0 = 78.1 MB. XHTML-paragraphs-only PDF output: inferred from Tika/PDFBox design, not verified on an official page.

findings.claim: Option 6 — Mistral OCR / PaddleOCR-VL as the structure source: Mistral OCR does emit real structure — markdown with heading hierarchy, tables as markdown or HTML (table_format param), block-level bounding boxes and confidence scores — so 'route every PDF through OCR' would technically consolidate parsing. But cost and posture kill it as the default path: $4 per 1,000 pages ($2 batch) on OCR 4, and it means shipping every legal document to an external API — acceptable as the PRD's *scanned-doc fallback* (PRD.md:234) but contrary to a self-hosted BYOK legal product as the mandatory path for born-digital documents PyMuPDF already reads locally; PRD DE-271 itself flags Mistral OCR as 'paid; not air-gappable' (PRD.md:2782). The air-gapped twin PaddleOCR-VL (PRD.md:283 already names it) is Apache-2.0 weights, 0.9B-param VLM emitting structured markdown + HTML tables, but official install guidance is paddlepaddle-gpu/CUDA; CPU inference of a 0.9B VLM per page is impractical at ingestion scale (inferred), and it would add a Paddle runtime rivaling the Docling footprint. Consolidation verdict: keep both exactly where the PRD put them — scanned-doc lane only.
findings.evidence: docs.mistral.ai basic_ocr: markdown output, table_format null/markdown/html, include_blocks bounding boxes, confidence scores; mistral.ai pricing via search: OCR 4 $4/1k pages, $2 batch; huggingface.co/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR-VL: apache-2.0 weights, markdown/JSON output, GPU/CUDA install examples; docs/PRD.md:234, :283, :2782, :5062.

findings.claim: Option 7 — Docling 2.x CPU-only, for the comparison table: MIT code (models' licenses vary), IBM Research origin now LF AI & Data Foundation — governance is strong; cadence is extremely fast (v2.120.1 on 2026-08-14, multiple releases monthly, which is itself a churn cost against our '>=1.16,<2' style pinning, api/pyproject.toml:92). Capability is the fullest of any option: layout analysis, reading order, TableFormer table structure, code/formula detection, native+scanned PDFs with pluggable OCR engines. CPU-only is officially supported via the PyTorch CPU wheel index ('pip install docling --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu'), which would eliminate the twelve nvidia-* packages (1.88 GB of our 2.91 GB, given); remaining footprint = CPU torch + torchvision + transformers + deps, estimated ~1-1.3 GB installed, plus the ~696 MB HF model downloads (estimate inferred; official docs publish no size number). So the honest CPU-Docling number is roughly 1.5-2 GB total and tens of packages — the cheapest way to keep Docling, but still ~30-40x pymupdf4llm's marginal cost.
findings.evidence: PyPI docling: v2.120.1 2026-08-14, MIT, LF AI & Data, layout/reading-order/TableFormer/OCR-engines; docling installation docs: '--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu' for cpu-only Linux; repo givens: api/pyproject.toml:92 'docling>=1.16,<2', 80 Docling-exclusive packages / 2.91 GB / 1.88 GB nvidia-* / ~696 MB models (given). Size of CPU-only install: inferred estimate.

findings.claim: PRD engagement: the repo has already reasoned about this landscape in DE-271 (docs/PRD.md:2778-2784) — it tiers Docling as a structural-risk dep with 'alternatives exist but with different output shapes' and names 'Apache Tika + custom parser layer' as the abandonment fallback, and PRD.md:234/:283 already position Mistral OCR (paid, not air-gappable) with PaddleOCR-VL as the air-gapped substitute. What DE-271 does NOT contemplate is the actual observed state — Docling never having worked (given: 6/6 docling=fallback) and nothing reading structured_content — which converts the question from 'fallback if abandoned' to 'was the dependency ever load-bearing'; and its Tika fallback overstates Tika's PDF-structure capability (text, not layout). Any memo should amend DE-271 rather than silently diverge from it.
findings.evidence: docs/PRD.md:2778 (DE-271 header), :2782 ('Docling (parser correctness; alternatives exist...)', 'Mistral OCR API (paid; not air-gappable)'), :2784 (Tika fallback), :234, :283; givens re docling=fallback and unread structured_content.

q4b.bottom_line: For "structure for legal contracts on CPU in a self-hosted image," only two options are credible: (1) pymupdf4llm — headings, tables, and reading order in markdown for ~45 MB marginal SBOM cost (pymupdf4llm 176 KB + pymupdf-layout ~43 MB), same Artifex AGPL/commercial license we already carry, no GPU, active releases — the clear default; and (2) Docling 2.x CPU-only as the high-capability runner-up if TableFormer-grade table structure ever becomes load-bearing, at an inferred ~1.5-2 GB / tens-of-packages cost and a fast-churn release cadence. Eliminated: marker (OpenRAIL-M weight license with a $5M revenue cap is incompatible with shipping in an open-source self-hosted product), unstructured (structure requires its hi_res model stack — a smaller Docling, worse licensed-capability ratio than pymupdf4llm), pdfplumber/camelot (tables only, no headings — complements not replacements), Tika (Apache-2.0 and cheap at ~78 MB + JVM, but PDFBox gives paragraphs of XHTML, not structure — it duplicates PyMuPDF, and DE-271's fallback claim should be softened accordingly), and routing everything through Mistral OCR/PaddleOCR-VL (real markdown structure, but $4/1k pages plus sending every contract to an external API — or a GPU-class Paddle stack — for documents PyMuPDF already reads locally; keep both confined to the scanned-doc lane the PRD already defines).

advisories.bottom_line: The claim "four HIGH advisories cover Docling 1.20.0" is TRUE — verified directly against the OSV API for docling==1.20.0. Exactly four unique advisories cover it, and all four are HIGH: CVE-2026-31248 (METS XXE, 7.5, no explicit fix version), CVE-2026-31247 (JATS XXE, 7.5, no explicit fix version), CVE-2026-44017 (EasyOCR Zip Slip, HIGH, fixed 2.91.0), CVE-2026-47214 (HTML backend URI/path handling, 7.1, fixed 2.94.0); a listing that counts the PYSEC aliases separately would misreport 8. Latest 2.x (2.120.1) has zero open OSV advisories, so upgrading clears all four, though the two XXE advisories close by absence-of-flag (last_affected 2.61.0) rather than an explicit fixed version. Note the two advisories fixed in 2.x require 2.91.0/2.94.0 — an upgrade merely into early 2.x would not clear them.
